messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] two-stage analyses
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ian:

Thanks for the email.  Yes, that's what I'd usually do too.  We'd fit a first step model in SAS or R and get lsmeans as breeding values and use these is subsequent genetic mapping analyses.  The challenge in these new experiments is that they are unreplicated - single plant per genotype - so, we're really limited to using the kinship matrix to estimate the breeding value.  Of course, we're not propagating the uncertainty in the blup and I'd agree that BLUPing the Blups seems a bad idea (given shrinkage).  I'm aware of some of Piepho's work and will see if I can dig into some of these papers for guidance too.  Any guess on publication date of the Piepho papers on staged analyses?

Tom

On Wednesday, September 30, 2020 at 11:46:36 AM UTC-5 Mac wrote:
> Hi Tom,
>
> I'm influenced by Hans-Peter Piepho who is definitely against BLUPing the BLUPs, and has published to this effect I think. This is more for GWAS than linkage analysis, but I guess similar arguments apply. Can you use weighted BLUEs in the second stage instead? You would then map these with a kinship matrix plus testing individual markers as fixed effects. I think that's what Hans-Peter would do. Against that, if you use empirical significance thresholds for your mapping, should it matter that much what you do?
>
> Best wishes,
>
> Ian
>
> On Mon, 28 Sep 2020 at 22:01, tom <tjue...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi R/qtl group;
> >
> > I’m emailing to get your opinion on a few analysis ideas.  I’m especially interested in hearing your thoughts and opinions about the use of “multiple stage” approaches to increase power in mapping.  We’ve been doing QTL and GWAS mapping in plants for many years. One thing that has always been a focus is doing our best to control background genetic and environmental effects to increase our power. We’ve used multiple QTL models, and more recently models with polygenic terms, to control for segregating QTL.  In terms of environmental effects, we’ll often include covariates associated with the experimental design like blocks, benches, trays, or even x y spatial coordinates.  These analyses are often completed first – followed by a secondary analysis in Rqtl based on the residuals, lsmeans, or blups from a prior statistical analysis. In a similar vein, we usually complete QTL mapping using RIL means determined from a first stage analysis (and leaving behind the within RIL variance).
> >
> > Several of our recent projects have utilized unreplicated plantings of experimental crosses or outbred GWAS panels.  In these cases, we have a single plant/genotype that has been phenotyped, sequenced, and planted in a grid with other unreplicated genotypes and some “checks” (replicated controls) in the field.  For mapping studies, this is fine as we can think of the unit of replication as the allele and can simply run our mapping as you would for an unreplicated F2 or a human GWAS study. However, we’d still like to calculate variance components and h2 (commonly reported for quantitative genetic studies) as well as control for environmental variance when possible. Recently, we’ve used linear mixed models and a relationship matrix to partition Va, Ve, and to estimate narrow-sense heritability in these unreplicated studies. We can also get “blup” estimates of the breeding values from these models.  My question is whether it is appropriate or valid to use the blups based on kinship in subsequent genetic mapping analyses. We’ve tried this and see marked increase in LOD scores and often detect many more QTL. On the one hand, I’d expect this as we should see an increase in power by reducing Ve and focusing on genetic values, especially for traits with relatively low h2. However, I’m a bit concerned that it’s circular in that the markers are used to estimate kinship from the first stage and used again in the mapping.  It might not be a terrible concern because the markers are used in aggregate for the kinship based mixed model and probably aren’t predictive of any single genotype in the mapping analysis. However, I’m old enough to be concerned when things look too good to be true.
> >
> > Has anyone seen this type of two-staged analysis?  Do you think the use of a marker-based kinship to estimate breeding values will create bias or problems with subsequent mapping?
> >
> > I’ve love to hear your thoughts,
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Tom

Hi Tom,
I was probably thinking of this:
"In stage-wise analysis, it is crucial to model genotypes by fixed effects throughout all stages except the last where genotypes are fixed or random depending on the objective of the analysis (e.g., random for
GBLUP, fixed for obtaining variety means, fixed and random for GWAS) (Piepho et al., 2012) "
The reference is
Piepho, H.-P., M¨ohring, J., Schulz-Streeck, T. and Ogutu, J.O. (2012). A stage-wise approach for
analysis of multi-environment trials. Biometrical Journal 54, 844–860.

and the quote is from Mackay, I., Piepho, H.P. and Garcia, A.A.F., 2019. Statistical methods for plant breeding. Handbook of Statistical Genomics: Two Volume Set, pp.501-20.
I remember he was keen on getting this point across. I'm sure he would answer any queries directly if you contacted him.

Best wishes,
Ian

messages.subject: Re: LOD score list from stepwiseqtl
messages.body_plain:
The data structures are a bit of a mess; sorry.

The lod profiles are stored in the qtl object as an attribute named "lodprofile", which can be retrieved with the function attr(). It is a list, with each component corresponding to a different QTL and being a three-column data frame with chromosome, position, and profile LOD score. You can use do.call("rbind", ....) to paste them together into a single data frame.

Here's an example:

    library(qtl)
    data(fake.bc)
    fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc, step=1)
    out <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk")
    qtl <- makeqtl(fake.bc, chr=c(2,5), pos=c(33,17), what="prob")
    rqtl <- refineqtl(fake.bc, qtl=qtl, keeplodprofile=TRUE, method="hk")
    lodprof_list <- attr(rqtl, "lodprofile")
    lodprof_df <- do.call("rbind", lodprof_list)

karl

messages.subject: Re: Parallel processing - R/QTL
messages.body_plain:
Could you say more precisely what you are doing?

Are you using comparegeno()? If so, then no, we have not implemented that for parallel computing.
But the related function in R/qtl2 is implemented to use multiple CPUs, so you could do:

  library(qtl2)
  mycross2 <- convert2cross2(mycross)
  d <- compare_geno(mycross2, cores=0)

But this just looks at the proportion of matching genotypes among typed markers. You might instead want to use the estimated kinship matrix as a measure of similarity.

  pr <- calc_genoprob(mycross2, error_prob=0.002, cores=0)
  k <- calc_kinship(pr, cores=0)

karl

messages.body_plain:
Ah, of course; sorry. est.map() and inter-marker distances.

est.map() does use multiple cores, but only by putting each chromosome on a different core. For the analysis of a single chromosome, there is no speed up.

If there were no missing genotype data, the map estimation would be quite fast. Here is an ad hoc method that I've found to work, to speed things up in the case of many markers:

  - fill.geno() to fill in missing data, in a temporary version of the cross
  - estimate the map distances with that
  - use that estimated map as an improved starting point with the real data.

    mycross_filled <- fill.geno(mycross)
    temp_map <- est.map(mycross_filled)
    mycross <- replacemap(mycross, temp_map)
    map <- est.map(mycross)

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dr. Broman,

I created a linkage map from a F2 population genotyped by WGS.
If I use physical position for marker ordering, then the map length looks good and the results seems ok but the issue is the population I used is quite different from the reference genome in which the alignment was performed.
I want to point out few regions of conflict between reference and my population even at the risk of inflating the map a bit.
So, I tried to order markers without the use of physical position and the initial order given by orderMarkers(mapthis, chr=1, use.ripple = FALSE) doesnot look that good and without use.ripple=FALSE, it doesn't even give me results for the markers I have (~2500).

rip2 <- ripple(mapthis, chr=1, window=3)
summary(rip2)

summary(rip5lik)

rip5lik is taking a lot of time even at window size of 3 and looks like the order isn't as accurate.
Is there a way to order markers by physical position and still look for signs of inversions or rearrangement in R/qtl?

Thanks,

Prashant

messages.subject: Inflated Linkage Map
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I just have a quick question (hopefully). I have a 6th generation RIL population and am trying to make a linkage map, but the map being produced is pretty inflated relative to what's been done in the literature (with closely related/the same organisms). For example, a LG with ~1000 markers will span ~1500 cm. I have a feeling this is due to residual heterozygosity... when I summary my cross, about 25% of my markers are missing/heterozygous. So, can residual heterozygosity cause inflated linkage maps? If so, is there somehow I can deal with this residual heterozygosity? I've been pretty strict with my variant filtering (before I even got into rQTL, i.e. at the vcf stage) but I'm pretty new to QTL mapping, so any assistance is appreciated!

I've followed all the filtering steps that are provided with the package, but aside from dropping about half our inds, I'm not sure what else to do.

Cheers,
Alex
